name: Shoot / Aim
subtitle: Aiming, hitting, and resource management create a closed loop; the core lies in hit feedback and risk-reward.
demoRuleHint: Rule: Aim → Fire → Hit determination → Feedback (knockback/explosion/score) → Cooldown/Reload
problemsSolved: Turn hit detection and feedback into a learnable rhythmic window (why hitting feels good).
Use constraints like ammo, recoil, and spread to control erratic shots and unlimited output.
Make pressure come from interpretable targets and rhythm, not just monster stacking.
Balancing ammo limits and output: too much ammo leads to overkill and lack of rhythm; too little ammo forces frequent reloading, breaking combo flow.
Balancing recoil and accuracy: excessive recoil makes shooting unstable and reduces combos; weak recoil makes players too precise, diminishing challenge.
Overly precise shooting weakens game rhythm: when players can easily hit all targets, the game loses tension and players may stop actively seeking dodge or strategy.
learningGoals: Beginner: understand the minimal loop — aim → fire → hit judgment → feedback → cooldown/reload — and reproduce one hit and one reload in the demo
Intermediate: write the trajectory and occlusion contract (hit judgment, spread model, ammo economy) and shape handling difficulty with fire rate and recoil
Advanced: design target-spawn rhythm and pressure curves, and verify shooting feel with accuracy distribution and reload-timing distribution
minimalRules: Hit: ray or projectile detection and occlusion.
systemLoopHint: Input (aim/fire) → Resolution (hit/occlusion) → Feedback (damage/recoil) → Resource change (cooldown/ammo) → New target.

combos.effect: Movement creates windows of opportunity, forming a high-pressure loop.
Accumulate resources through hits/kills to drive weapon progression.
Projectile trajectories interact with the environment, expanding strategic space.

advancedWarnings: Weak hit feedback makes shooting feel like 'air shots'.
Unexplained recoil and spread break the learning curve.
Inconsistent occlusion rules cause strong frustration.
advancedAlgoRefs: Hit detection: rays/projectiles, collision layers, hitboxes.
Spawn generation: enemy refresh rhythm and wave design.

demoLab.title: Ammo Rhythm Experiment
demoLab.action: Spam "Fire (primary)" until ammo runs dry, watch accuracy decay, then hit "Reload (secondary)" to refill
demoLab.observe: Empty ammo forces a reload window — resource cuts the output rhythm. Accuracy visibly drops while spraying: the ammo constraint turns "infinite output" into "every trigger pull has an opportunity cost"

demoLab.title: Difficulty Contrast
demoLab.action: On easy vs hard, click "Advance 1 Step" 10 steps each and compare targets and accuracy
demoLab.observe: Difficulty changes spawn pressure: on hard, targets pile up faster and the same fire rate dilutes accuracy. The difficulty knob is a stress test on hit rate — accuracy shifts from a feel-good metric to a survival metric

demoLab.title: Disciplined Fire Experiment
demoLab.action: Fire only once every 3 ticks (click "Advance 1 Step" three times, then "Fire (primary)"), and after 20 steps compare accuracy with experiment one
demoLab.observe: Disciplined fire scores markedly higher accuracy than spraying — depth in a shooter comes from precision, not volume. That is why production designs punish mindless rapid fire with spread/recoil: perfect accuracy would kill the tension

intro.what: Aim at the target and fire — hits score, ammo is limited. Shooters, target-range games, and FPS titles are all built on this.
intro.feel: The reticle settles on a target, you squeeze the trigger, and the hit feedback bursts; when the mag runs dry you scramble to reload — lose the rhythm for a second and targets pile up into a mountain.
intro.why: "How juice gets manufactured" is nowhere more visible than in shooting — hit feedback, ammo constraints, and risk-reward are required courses in feedback design.

concept: Shooting play is an extremely short reward loop: aim, fire, hit judgment, feedback burst — every trigger pull is an evaluable micro-decision. The hard part is not the hit — it is the explainability of constraints: ammo and cooldowns turn infinite output into rhythm management, while spread and recoil turn "firing a lot" into "firing well." A gun "feels good in the hand" when the reason behind every hit and every miss is clearly visible.
designNotes: Ammo is a pacing valve, not resource packaging: the reload window forcibly interrupts the output beat — too much ammo and mindless spraying kills tension, too little and combos break constantly. Mag size is the heartbeat rate of a shooter.

Spraying must be punished (counterintuitively punishing high-frequency play): empty shots cost accuracy, spread punishes rapid fire — spraying without a price destroys the value of precision. Shooting depth comes from restraint, not firepower.
Weak hit feedback is shooting at air: knockback, sound, and the instant score burst ARE the juice — no matter how accurate the judgment is, muted feedback never lets players feel their own skill.
